intro.text: Almost nothing on the SR-71 came off the shelf: not the fuel, the engines, the metal, the navigation or the suits its crews wore. It was designed to cruise at Mach 3.2 and cleared to 85,000 feet. These are its systems, as the flight manual the Air Force flew it by and the NASA reports written about it describe them.

sections.title: The inlet did most of the work

paras.text: At cruise the J58 was not the main source of thrust. A Lockheed breakdown quoted by NASA historian Peter Merlin gives the inlet 54 percent of the thrust at Mach 3, the ejector nozzle behind the engine 29 percent and the engine itself 17 percent. At Mach 2.2 the engine still supplied 73 percent. NASA's own fact sheet puts it plainly: less than 20 percent of the thrust at Mach 3 came from the engine.

Each inlet is a mixed-compression design with a spike that moves. The spike is locked forward on the ground and below 30,000 feet. From Mach 1.6 it moves aft about 1-5/8 inches for every 0.1 Mach, to about 26 inches. As it retracts, the throat closes to 54 percent of its Mach 1.6 area while the air the inlet captures more than doubles.

Two rings of doors keep the shock wave where it belongs. Forward bypass doors just behind the throat spill air overboard to hold the shock at the throat; aft bypass doors just ahead of the engine send air around it to the ejector. If the shock is thrown out of the inlet, an unstart, a sensor sees compressor inlet pressure fall by more than 23 percent, opens the forward bypass fully and drives the spike forward by up to 15 inches, then retracts it 3.75 seconds later.

NASA's YF-12 flights measured how fast an unstart happens: the shock reached the spike tip in about a hundredth of a second. Between Mach 2.3 and 2.6 an unstart was violent enough to snap a pilot's head and helmet against the inside of the canopy.

figures.caption: Flight manual Figure 1-21: the inlet's doors and airflow at each stage of flight, from standstill to Mach 3.2.
NASA's cutaway of the inlet: 16 forward bypass doors, 24 aft bypass doors, 32 shock trap tubes and 4 spike struts. Drawn for the YF-12 program, which used the same inlet.
Looking into the left inlet of SR-71A 61-7971 at the Evergreen Aviation & Space Museum.

sections.title: The J58, built to burn in afterburner for hours

paras.text: Two Pratt & Whitney J58s, company designation JT11D-20, each rated at 34,000 lb of thrust in maximum afterburner at sea level. The 32,500 lb often quoted belongs to the early engine with fixed inlet guide vanes; the A-12's version was rated at 31,500 lb.

Its compressor has nine stages and a pressure ratio of only 8.8 to 1, because at cruise the inlet does most of the compressing. From about Mach 1.8 to 2.0, air bled from the fourth stage flows through six tubes around the rest of the engine and straight into the afterburner.
It was designed for Mach 3.2 with both full military power and afterburner run continuously, and its own fuel served as the hydraulic fluid for the nozzle, guide vanes and bleeds, at up to 1,800 psi.

JP-7 is so hard to light that a lit match will not ignite it. The engines are lit chemically instead, with triethylborane, which burns on contact with air. Each engine carries enough for at least 16 shots, and a counter beside each throttle counts them down.
Turning a J58 over to start took more than 600 horsepower. Lockheed's answer was a cart carrying two Buick racing car engines, geared together to the engine's starter drive.

figures.caption: Flight manual Figure 1-2: the JT11D-20 with 26 numbered parts, among them the bypass tubes that carry fourth-stage air to the afterburner.
A J58 in an altitude test chamber at NASA's Lewis Research Center, March 1974.
A J58 on its stand at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force, with its bypass ducts and plumbing on the outside.
A start cart at the Hill Aerospace Museum, Utah, which calls it the AG330. A drive shaft from the cart spins the engine through its gearbox.

sections.title: Two cockpits, and only one has a stick

paras.text: The pilot's centre panel alone has 50 numbered items in the flight manual. The attitude director indicator sits in the middle. The inlet controls are grouped at the lower left: spike and forward bypass knobs graduated in Mach from 1.4 to 3.2, and a spike position indicator reading 0 to 26 inches. The engine instruments run down the right: tachometers, exhaust gas temperature, nozzle position, fuel flow and oil pressure.
A triple display indicator shows speed, altitude and Mach in digits. Its altitude window reads to 99,950 feet and drops the first digit above 100,000.

Behind the pilot sits the reconnaissance systems officer, who has no flight controls: a downward-looking viewsight at the top of the panel, a radar display below it, and the sensor and navigation panels on the consoles.

The astro-inertial navigation system steers by the stars, day and night. A telescope behind the rear cockpit looks up through a window and tracks stars from a 61-star catalogue; in astro-inertial mode the expected position error is 0.3 nautical miles for up to 10 hours.

Flight manual Figure 1-17: the reconnaissance systems officer's panel, viewsight at the top.
The rear cockpit of 61-7975 from above, with its seat removed.

paras.text: At cruise the skin averaged 462 to 622 °F and reached 1,050 °F on the nacelles. Titanium alloys make up 93 percent of the structural weight.

The wing skins are corrugated chordwise so they can expand without buckling. Kelly Johnson wrote that at design heating the corrugations merely deepened by a few thousandths of an inch. The airframe as a whole grows by up to four inches in length.
It is painted black to radiate heat away. In the cockpit the outer glass reached 420 °F while the cooling air came in at minus 40 °F.

figures.caption: Upper surface temperatures of the YF-12A at Mach 3 cruise, 250 to 600 °F: hottest on the wing edges and nacelles, coolest over the fuel tanks.
The YF-12A wing structure, with chordwise corrugated skins that let it grow as it heats.

sections.title: Fuel as coolant, nitrogen as insurance

paras.text: Eight tanks hold 12,219 US gallons, 80,280 lb of JP-7. Before it is burned, the fuel cools the air conditioning, the hydraulic fluid and the engine oil; once it passes 290 °F, the hottest fuel is sent back to tank 4 instead of to the engines.
Liquid nitrogen, 262 liters in three flasks, pressurises the tanks and fills the space above the hot fuel so it cannot ignite. Without it the aircraft is limited to Mach 2.6.
In the air it took on fuel at about 6,000 lb a minute, every tank filling at once in 12 to 15 minutes, from a dedicated fleet of KC-135Q tankers.

figures.caption: Flight manual Figure 1-32: the eight tanks and what each holds.
SR-71 61-7974 moves in behind KC-135Q 59-1513 to refuel, 1983.

paras.text: Both crew sat on Lockheed SR-1 rocket ejection seats, usable from zero speed and altitude to the edge of the flight envelope. Pulling the D-ring jettisons the canopy and then fires the catapult; the rocket lights as the seat clears the sills, a drogue opens from the headrest, and at 15,000 feet the seat throws its occupant clear before a 35-foot parachute opens.
From late 1978 until 1996 they flew in David Clark S1030 full-pressure suits: six layers that hold 3.5 psi if the cockpit loses pressure.

figures.caption: Flight manual Figure 1-83: the SR-1 ejection seat.
A NASA SR-71 crew in full-pressure suits, 1991.

model.text: Article 121 built this model in Blender from NASA Dryden's vector three-view of the SR-71A, put on true scale with the fuselage stations in a NASA wind-tunnel report (nose at station 102, tail cone at 1355). The cross-sections are measured from a Lockheed lines drawing whose original has not yet been traced to a government archive. Its outline overlaps NASA's drawing by 97.6 percent in plan view and 95.4 percent in side view. It is a reconstruction, not a scan: markings, panel lines, landing gear and the cockpit interiors are not modelled yet.

nose-section.title: Nose section
nose-section.text: The nose ahead of the cockpits could be exchanged. SR-71s flew with chined noses carrying the CAPRE side-looking radar, the optical bar camera or the ASARS radar; the ASARS nose had a one-piece quartz and polyimide radome-chine.

pitot-probe.title: Pitot-static probe
pitot-probe.text: The pitot-static boom on the nose tip, as drawn on NASA's three-view.

forward-fuselage.title: Forward fuselage and cockpits
forward-fuselage.text: Two cockpits in tandem, the pilot forward and the reconnaissance systems officer behind, each under its own canopy. The cockpits held a 26,000 ft or 10,000 ft pressure schedule.

canopy-glass.title: Windshield and canopy glass
canopy-glass.text: At cruise the outer glass reached 420 °F while the crew's cooling air came in at minus 40 °F.

chine-forebody.title: Chine forebody
chine-forebody.text: The chines run from the nose to the wing and carried almost 20 percent of the lift. The bays inside them carried sensors and equipment, listed on the flight manual's bay locator.

centre-body.title: Centre body and fuel
centre-body.text: The centre body carries the wing through and holds most of the fuel: eight tanks, 80,280 lb of JP-7. The fuel cooled the cockpit air, the hydraulics and the engine oil before it was burned.

tail-cone.title: Tail cone
tail-cone.text: The fuselage ends in a tail cone behind the wing. Like the chines, wing edges, spike cones and fins, it used heat-resistant non-metallic laminates in places.

inner-wing.title: Inner wing
inner-wing.text: A multispar, multirib wing whose skins are corrugated chordwise so they can grow with heat without buckling; at design heating the corrugations deepened by only a few thousandths of an inch. Inboard elevons on the trailing edge.

outer-wing.title: Outer wing
outer-wing.text: Outboard of the nacelles the leading edge droops in conical camber. The outboard elevons, each moved by 14 actuating cylinders, give pitch and roll control.

nacelle.title: Nacelle
nacelle.text: Inlet, engine and ejector nozzle in one nacelle, working as one propulsion system. At Mach 3 the inlet produced 54 percent of the thrust, the ejector 29 percent and the J58 itself 17 percent.

inlet-duct.title: Inlet duct
inlet-duct.text: The duct from the cowl lip, 29.38 in in radius, to the engine face about 5.4 cowl radii behind it. Bypass doors in its walls held the shock wave at the throat.

spike.title: Inlet spike
spike.text: Locked forward below 30,000 feet; from Mach 1.6 it moves aft about 1-5/8 inches per 0.1 Mach, to about 26 inches, closing the throat to 54 percent of its Mach 1.6 area.

j58.title: Pratt & Whitney J58
j58.text: JT11D-20 bleed-bypass turbojet with afterburner, 34,000 lbf in maximum afterburner. A nine-stage compressor with a pressure ratio of only 8.8 to 1, eight burner cans and a two-stage turbine. Shape here is representative, after the flight manual cutaway.

bypass-tubes.title: Bleed bypass tubes
bypass-tubes.text: From about Mach 1.8 to 2.0, air bled from the fourth compressor stage runs through six tubes around the rest of the engine straight into the afterburner. Positions here are representative.

ejector.title: Ejector nozzle
ejector.text: An airframe-mounted ejector around the afterburner: flaps of Hastelloy X on a Rene 41 ring, 1,400 °F inside and 1,600 °F outside in afterburner. At Mach 3 it made 29 percent of the thrust.

fin.title: Fin and rudder
fin.text: All-moving rudders on fixed stub fins on top of the nacelles, each canted inward 15 degrees, driven by dual A and B hydraulic servos.
